## Source and method

Video Mw60FH5iflI = Adam Brown (Google DeepMind "Blueshift" lead / Stanford physicist), **"Training Sand to Think: Artificial General Intelligence & Future of Physics"** — the Aspen Center for Physics public lecture (Aspen Institute, Paepcke Auditorium). Note there are TWO uploads of essentially this talk: `Mw60FH5iflI` (the one you asked about) and `Rs5_Q7nUVQ8` ("...and the Future of Science"). Aspen Public Radio lists airings 2026-01-16 and 2026-02-04; a YouTube upload is dated 2026-06-04.

WebFetch on YouTube and every transcript mirror (youtubetranscript.com, youtubetotranscript, tactiq, notegpt, youtube-transcript.io) returned 403 or the tool's landing page. I got the real captions with **`yt-dlp --extractor-args "youtube:player_client=mweb" --skip-download --write-auto-subs --sub-langs "en.*"`** (default/web/tv/ios/android clients all failed with "Precondition check failed"; `mweb` worked). Files: `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-tobias-Projects-ai-agents-seminar/ef6885d8-66f2-4d77-bc0f-7aa7ccdcf963/scratchpad/ab/t_mweb.en-orig.srt` (raw) and `.../ab/clean.txt` (deduped, ~10,090 words). **Caveat: these are auto-generated ASR captions, so quotes below are verbatim-from-captions, not verbatim-from-Brown.** Wording is reliable; exact punctuation is not. I could not obtain the actual slide images, so axis styling below is inferred from what he says about the plots, not read off a slide.

## ANSWER: the "PhD-level questions" plot is **GPQA**

The y-axis benchmark for the PhD-level-questions plot is **GPQA** (he says just "GPQA"; the captions never say "Diamond", but the ~70% expert baseline he quotes is the GPQA Diamond expert number, so it is the Diamond subset). It is **not** HLE — HLE appears later and only as a throwaway joke, with no plot of its own.

Key caption quotes:
- "I talked about high school maths. Now, let's talk about graduate science. This is a considerably trickier benchmark. Uh a benchmark made later and solved later. Um GPQA, it's called. This is meant to be uh imitating the kind of problems you would face as a first-year graduate student working towards your PhD."
- "Um PhDs PhD level experts scored about 70%."
- "and uh yeah, GPQA, a much harder benchmark. Um and correspondingly, **this graph is shifted about a year compared to the the math benchmark** I was describing before. **We were essentially random guessing until about the beginning of 2024.** Uh and then over the course of 2024 and 2025, we went from **random guessing past expert human level, and now they achieve essentially perfect score.**"
- "I mean, that's it. **GPQA is dead.** It has once again suffered the fate of all benchmarks, uh and uh it is no longer useful cuz it is too easy."

## Plot design (enough to reproduce)

It is a **series of same-format benchmark-saturation plots**, one per benchmark, not one combined plot:
- **x-axis: calendar date**, roughly 2021 → 2026 (he repeatedly anchors "the state of the art exactly 4 years ago today", "beginning of 2024", "over the course of 2024 and 2025"). Linear.
- **y-axis: benchmark accuracy in percent, 0–100. LINEAR, not log.** The scale is pinned by two horizontal reference lines that only make sense on a percent axis:
  - a **random-guessing floor** (GPQA is 4-way multiple choice → ~25%),
  - a **human-expert line** (**GPQA: ~70% for PhD-level experts**; on the MATH plot: **40% for a "computer science PhD student who does not especially like mathematics"** and **90% for a "three-time International Math Olympiad gold medalist"**, i.e. "peak human").
- **Shape: sigmoid / S-curve saturating at 100%.** Flat at random-guessing → steep rise → blows straight through the human-expert line → pinned at "essentially perfect". Markers are individual named models over time (he names Minerva at 50%, "Max Math" at 90% by mid-2024, then off-the-shelf LLMs near-perfect 6 months later).
- The **rhetorical device is the horizontal shift**: the GPQA curve is the MATH curve **translated ~1 year to the right**. He walks up a ladder of benchmarks (MATH → MATH level-5 hardest 20% → GPQA → HLE → IMO), each one "made later and solved later", each dying the same death: "way too hard to be a useful marker of progress to being way too easy to be a useful marker of progress."

## The headline claim (the actual "models vs time" line)

His headline quantitative claim is an **education-level-vs-time line**, drawn across the benchmark ladder rather than on a single benchmark:

- "we can plot it forward a few more years as they've at least as far as exam taking goes, **accelerated from preschool, past elementary school, high school, college, and they're now operating at the PhD level**."
- **"a good rule of thumb is that we're moving about four times as fast as a human student moves. For every year that passes, we advance four years into the future."** ← this is the money quote and the slope of his line: **4 grade-years of capability per calendar year**.

## Two other straight-line plots in the talk (don't conflate them with the GPQA one)

1. **Log-scale plots** exist in the talk but are about *inputs*, not benchmark scores: Moore's law ("the price of compute has been dropping uh exponentially, making a linear line on a on a logarithmic plot"), training FLOPs ("increased by a factor of **four uh every year since 2010**"), and training spend ("**2.7x per year** over the last decade", ~$0.5M in 2020 → ~$300M last year). He explicitly says he shows Moore's law "to emphasize how little this has to do with the subject of today's talk" — his talk is only the last ~5 years, the far right edge. He also notes **algorithmic progress**, not compute, is "the number one most important contributor".
2. **The chess-Elo reveal.** He draws a hand-wavy "strength of LLMs vs time" line with a deliberately "poorly defined Y axis", then reveals: "**I took this line from something completely different. That line uh I took from chess computers**... the Y axis is **Elo**... the X axis is the the year... that was a **straight line uh going up and it just kept going up**... notably it kept going up **well past peak human**." He then maps chess's **four eras — toy → tool → centaur ("central") → superhuman** — onto AI-for-physics, arguing we're ~30 years behind chess and that "there was nothing special about peak human strength at chess. It just got better and better and better."

His framing throughout: "lines that really have no business being straight, but nevertheless are — and [I] invite you to imagine what will happen if those lines continue to be straight for just a little bit longer."

Closing claim: cost-to-serve a fixed level of intelligence has fallen "by many orders of magnitude", so "if you can make one AI Einstein, you can make a billion of them"; the next few years will be "a golden era of physics" / "the most exciting time to be a physicist... in recorded history".

## Caveats for a public talk
- No METR time-horizon plot, no ARC-AGI, no FrontierMath plot, no SWE-bench in this talk (searched: zero hits for "METR", "doubling", "horizon").
- Brown gives **no numeric GPQA model scores** — the plot is narrated qualitatively ("random guessing" → "essentially perfect"). If you want actual GPQA Diamond datapoints for a reproduction, you must source them separately (Epoch AI / Artificial Analysis), not from this talk.
- He is a Google DeepMind insider presenting DeepMind results (Minerva, "Max Math", IMO gold); treat the framing as vendor-adjacent even though the benchmarks are third-party.
- He preemptively rebuts contamination ("we do not believe that that is what is happening"), citing held-out look-alike problems and his own private hand-graded Stanford GR/QM graduate exams, on which models went to "100% accuracy" over ~18 months — "My benchmark sadly dead."

SOURCING / METHOD
- arcprize.org/leaderboard is a JS-rendered Next.js page; WebFetch returns no table. I recovered the leaderboard's own data files by reading /scripts/leaderboard/data.js, which fetches `/media/data/leaderboard/{v1,v2,v3}.json`. All records above are verbatim from those files (fetched 2026-07-12). Every JSON payload carries "generatedAt": "2026-07-09T19:48:54Z" — i.e. the board was regenerated the day GPT-5.6 landed. Model metadata (open-weight notes, paper URLs) is in /media/data/models.json.
- ALL scores above are the SEMI-PRIVATE eval split (datasetId v1_Semi_Private / v2_Semi_Private / v3_Semi_Private), which is what arcprize.org displays by default. The data.js file shows Public-Eval and Private-Eval splits also exist but are commented out. Do not mix splits.
- Evaluator is ARC Prize themselves (they run the semi-private eval); these are NOT vendor self-reported numbers. Third-party "systems" entries (Poetiq, Johan Land, J. Berman, E. Pang) are ARC-Prize-verified scaffolds built on a base model, not the base model alone — I excluded most of them to avoid confusion, but e.g. "GPT-5.2 (Refine.)" by Johan Land scores 72.90% on ARC-AGI-2 at $38.99/task and "Gemini 3 Pro (Refine.)" by Poetiq scores 54.00% at $30.568/task.

*** THE HEADLINE FINDING — THE TASK PREMISE IS NOW OUT OF DATE ***
ARC-AGI-2 is NO LONGER unsaturated. It is close to done.
- Current top: GPT-5.6 Sol (Max), 92.5%, $1.44/task, released 2026-07-09 (three days ago).
- Human Panel reference on ARC-AGI-2 is 100% (score: 1) at $17/task. So the frontier is within ~7.5 points of the human panel ceiling.
- The trajectory over the last ~7 months is steep, not steady-slow:
  2025-12-11 GPT-5.2 (xHigh) 52.9% -> 2026-02-12 Gemini 3 Deep Think 84.6% -> 2026-03-04 GPT-5.4 Pro (xHigh) 83.3% -> 2026-04-22 GPT-5.5 (xHigh) 85.0% -> 2026-07-09 GPT-5.6 Sol (Max) 92.5%.
  Note the plateau Feb–Apr 2026 (~83–85%) followed by a jump to 92.5% with GPT-5.6.
- If your talk needs an "unsaturated frontier benchmark", use ARC-AGI-3, not ARC-AGI-2. ARC-AGI-3 was announced 2026-03-25 (arcprize.org/blog) and the ENTIRE leaderboard tops out at 7.78% (GPT-5.6 Sol Max). Everything else is under 2.2%. That is the current wall.

COST COLLAPSE (a strong talk point)
- Cost per task for a given score has fallen dramatically. Gemini 3 Deep Think hit 84.58% on ARC-AGI-2 at $13.62/task (Feb 2026); GPT-5.6 Sol (Max) beats it at 92.5% for $1.44/task (Jul 2026) — ~9.5x cheaper and 8 points better in 5 months. GPT-5.4 Pro got 83.33% at $16.41/task; GPT-5.6 Sol (High) gets 85.42% at $0.74/task, ~22x cheaper.
- ARC-AGI-3 costs are reported as a TOTAL eval cost field ("cost"), NOT cost-per-task: GPT-5.6 Sol (Max) cost $25,064.11 for the run. Several entries are exactly 10000, which looks like a cost cap/placeholder rather than a measurement — treat ARC-AGI-3 costs with suspicion.

OPEN-WEIGHT MODELS
- Best open-weight model on ARC-AGI-2 is GLM-5.2 (Z.ai): 22.78% at $0.2501/task. On ARC-AGI-1 it gets 77.0% at $0.1916/task. Open weights confirmed independently (simonwillison.net/2026/jun/17/glm-52/, VentureBeat): "Z.ai released GLM-5.2 to their coding plan subscribers on June 13th, and then on June 16th released the full open weights under an MIT license."
- Kimi K2.5 (Moonshot) 11.81% ARC-AGI-2 / 65.33% ARC-AGI-1. ARC's own models.json metadata note calls it "an open-weight multimodal agentic model with 1 trillion parameters."
- The open/closed gap on ARC-AGI-2 is enormous and NOT closing: 92.5% (closed) vs 22.78% (best open) = ~70 point gap. This contrasts sharply with coding benchmarks where GLM-5.2 is near-frontier. Worth flagging as a benchmark-specific divergence.
- I marked Deepseek V3.2 and Minimax M2.5 weights as "unknown" — both vendors have an open-weight track record but I could not verify these specific releases within budget, and my training data is stale. Do not assert open weights for those two without checking. GLM-5 marked open with medium confidence (Z.ai line is open, but I only verified 5.2 directly).
- No open-weight model appears on the ARC-AGI-3 leaderboard at all.

DISCREPANCIES / CAVEATS THE ANALYST MUST KNOW
1. Release dates are INCONSISTENT between ARC's own files. Same model, different date in v1/v2 vs v3: Gemini 3.1 Pro (2026-02-19 in v1/v2, 2026-03-05 in v3); GPT-5.4 (2026-03-04 vs 2026-03-05); GPT-5.5 (2026-04-22 vs 2026-04-23); Grok 4.20 (2026-03-09 vs 2026-03-05). I used the date from whichever file each record came from. Use ARC's dates only as approximate.
2. Reasoning-effort ordering is NOT monotonic. On ARC-AGI-1, GPT-5.6 Sol (xHigh) scores 97.5% but Sol (Max) scores 96.5% — Max is WORSE than xHigh. Same for GPT-5.6 Luna on ARC-AGI-3 (xHigh 0.02% vs High 0.10% vs Max 0.18%). At the top of ARC-AGI-1 the scores are within eval noise (120-task semi-private set => ~0.83%/task). Do not over-read 1-2 point differences.
3. ARC-AGI-1 is fully saturated: Gemini 3.1 Pro (Preview) hits 98.0%, exactly tying the Human Panel and Stem Grad reference lines (both 98.0%). ARC-AGI-1 has no signal left — do not use it as a live frontier measure.
4. A third-party aggregator (agentmarketcap.ai, dated 2026-04-06/07-06) reports "GPT-5.5 leads the ARC-AGI-2 leaderboard with 85%, followed by GPT-5.4 Pro (83.3%) and Gemini 3.1 Pro (77.1%)". Those three numbers match ARC's data EXACTLY, but the ranking is stale — it predates the GPT-5.6 family (2026-07-09). Recording the discrepancy as instructed: the aggregator is not wrong, it is out of date. Use 92.5% (GPT-5.6 Sol Max) as the current top.
5. Human Panel on ARC-AGI-2 is stored as score: 1 (100%). Some ARC publications quote "average individual human performance ~60-66%" — that is a DIFFERENT metric (single human, not panel). Be explicit about which you cite.
6. I did not find an ARC Prize blog post analyzing GPT-5.6 yet; the most recent relevant posts are "ARC Prize 2026: ARC-AGI-3 Milestone Prize #1" (07.06.26) and "Analyzing GPT-5.5 & Opus 4.7 with ARC-AGI-3" (05.01.26). So there is no ARC narrative commentary on the 92.5% yet — it is fresh raw data.

Local working files (all in scratch): /tmp/arc_v1.json, /tmp/arc_v2.json, /tmp/arc_v3.json, /tmp/arc_models.json (raw fetched payloads); /tmp/out_v1.txt, /tmp/out_v2.txt, /tmp/out_v3.txt (full sorted tables — 170 ARC-AGI-1 rows, 172 ARC-AGI-2 rows, 22 ARC-AGI-3 rows, far more than the ~50 records emitted above).

=== GPQA DIAMOND SATURATION — THE HEADLINE ANSWER ===
Per Epoch AI's own standardized runs (not vendor claims), the FIRST model to exceed 90% on GPQA Diamond was **Gemini 3 Pro Preview, 92.61%, released 2025-11-18**. Verbatim CSV row: "gemini-3-pro-preview,0.9261363636363636,0.9261363636363636,2025-11-18,Google DeepMind".
It was followed within weeks by GPT-5.2 (xhigh) at 91.4% on 2025-12-11 and Claude Opus 4.6 (32K) at 90.53% on 2026-02-05; Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview hit 94.1% on 2026-02-19.
So: **GPQA Diamond effectively saturated in November–December 2025**, i.e. roughly 14 months after the reasoning-model era began (o1, Dec 2024, 76.8%).

Why "effectively saturated" is the right word, with quotes:
- Epoch's Gradient Update (2025-05-30) manually audited the benchmark and found "an overall invalid question rate of 15/198 = 8%" and wrote "I think it's likely that at least 90% of the benchmark is valid." That puts the EFFECTIVE CEILING at roughly 92%. Gemini 3 Pro (92.6%) and Gemini 3.1 Pro (94.1%) are AT OR ABOVE that estimated ceiling — the residual is now dominated by label noise, not capability.
- Same piece: "A specter looms whenever AI systems approach 100% on a benchmark: what if the rest of the benchmark is flawed?" and "Even if saturation has not yet come for GPQA, it's only a matter of time." (Written when SOTA was ~83%.)
- The "PhD-level" framing is now dead: Epoch's GPQA page states OpenAI "recruited PhD-level experts to answer questions in GPQA Diamond, and found that they scored 69.7%." Models passed the human-expert baseline with o1 in Dec 2024 (76.8%) and are now ~25 points above it. GPT-4 in Mar 2023 scored 35.7% — barely above the 25% random-guess floor.
- Good talk framing: 2023 GPT-4 35.7% → 2024 o1 76.8% → Nov 2025 Gemini 3 Pro 92.6% → Feb 2026 Gemini 3.1 Pro 94.1%, against a human PhD-expert baseline of 69.7% and an estimated ~92% validity ceiling.

SOURCE / METHOD
All records are from artificialanalysis.ai (AA runs these evals themselves — one methodology across open and closed models). Evaluator is "Artificial Analysis" for every record; none are vendor self-reported.

Data was obtained from four kinds of AA page:
1. /leaderboards/models — the master table (Model | Creator | AA Intelligence Index). This rendered fully and is the source for the bulk of Intelligence Index records. Quotes for these are the extracted table row.

4. /articles/<slug> — launch analyses. The GLM-5.2 article is the one place giving a FULL 9-benchmark breakdown for an open-weights model, so GLM-5.2 is the best open-vs-closed anchor in this dataset.

collectors.notes:
RECOMMENDATION (single best benchmark): **Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI)**, https://epoch.ai/eci, data at https://epoch.ai/data/eci_scores.csv. Runner-up / best single-benchmark percentage axis: **HLE as run by Artificial Analysis**. Use ECI as the headline curve and HLE (or CritPt, for a physics audience) as the concrete "what the score means" illustration.

WHY ECI:
1. It cannot saturate by construction. Epoch: "The Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) combines scores from many different AI benchmarks into a single 'general capability' scale, allowing comparisons between models even over timespans long enough for single benchmarks to reach saturation" and "Note that as with Elo scores, there is no maximum achievable ECI." It is an IRT/Elo-style latent-ability fit over 50+ benchmarks; saturated benchmarks are simply down-weighted and new ones swapped in.
2. Longest continuous series of any candidate: 193 dated models from 2023-02-24 (LLaMA-65B, 109.95) to 2026-07-09 (GPT-5.6 Sol pro/max, 161.61). Closed frontier: GPT-4 125.94 (2023-03) -> o1 142.67 (2024-12) -> GPT-5 150.0 (2025-08) -> GPT-5.2 Pro 154.56 (2025-12) -> GPT-5.4 Pro 157.71 (2026-03) -> GPT-5.5 Pro 160.56 (2026-04) -> GPT-5.6 Sol 161.61 (2026-07). ~+10.5 ECI points/year, and because ECI is a logit-scale ability, a linear ECI trend IS exponential improvement in odds-of-success — exactly the "steady exponential" claim you want to make, without a 100% ceiling artefact.
3. Open weights are first-class: the CSV has an explicit "Accessibility group" column (Open weights / Closed weights / Other). The open-weight frontier is a clean parallel curve: LLaMA-65B 109.95 (2023-02) -> Llama 3.1-405B 128.99 (2024-07) -> DeepSeek-R1 139.65 (2025-01) -> Qwen3-235B-Thinking 144.76 (2025-07) -> Kimi K2.5 148.24 (2026-01) -> Kimi K2.6 150.90 (2026-04) -> GLM-5.2 151.57 (2026-06). Today's open-weight frontier (151.6) sits ~10 ECI points behind the closed frontier (161.6), i.e. roughly where the closed frontier was around Aug-Oct 2025 => a ~9-11 month lag, and the gap has been roughly constant since 2024. That is a great, defensible slide.
4. Cadence: both Epoch (211 models) and Artificial Analysis (533 models, with release_date on each) let you plot releases-per-quarter directly. AA model counts by half-year: 2023-H1 1, 2023-H2 10, 2024-H1 19, 2024-H2 43, 2025-H1 98, 2025-H2 181, 2026-H1 159, and 21 already in the first 10 days of 2026-H2. Overlay this bar chart on the ECI frontier line and you have "rising capability AND accelerating cadence" in one figure. OpenAI shipped GPT-5.6 in three simultaneous variants (Sol/Terra/Luna) on 2026-07-09 — a nice cadence anecdote.

WHY NOT THE OTHERS (survey results):
- GPQA Diamond: SATURATED. Epoch top 94.6% (GPT-5.4 Pro); open-weight GLM-5.2 at 91.9%. Spread between frontier open and closed is ~3 points. Dead as a discriminator; only useful as a "here is what saturation looks like" foil.
- ARC-AGI-2: SATURATING FAST and the story is now over. ARC Prize semi-private: GPT-5.6 Sol (Max) 92.5% ($1.44/task) vs 2025 human panel 100%. Series starts Dec 2024 (o3 preview 4.0%), so no 2023 baseline. Superb visual (4% -> 92.5% in 19 months) but the headroom is gone, and open-weight coverage is thin and stale (GLM-5.2 22.8%, Kimi K2.5 11.8%, DeepSeek V3.2 4.0%) — the open/closed gap on ARC-AGI-2 is enormous and probably reflects effort/config, not just capability. ARC-AGI-3 launched (top score GPT-5.6 Sol Max 7.78%, at ~$25k total cost) but has only ~6 models, no open weights, no history: a floor, not a trend line.
- HLE: STRONGEST SINGLE BENCHMARK. AA-run (independent, standardised harness): top 53.3% (Claude Fable 5), 533 models scored incl. 315 open-weight. AA retro-scores old models, so the series really does start 2023-03 (GPT-4-era ~4-6%). Closed frontier: o1 7.7% (2024-12) -> o3 20.0% -> GPT-5 26.5% (2025-08) -> Gemini 3 Pro 37.2% (2025-11) -> Gemini 3.1 Pro 44.7% (2026-02) -> Fable 5 53.3% (2026-06). Open-weight frontier: Llama 2 ~5% -> DeepSeek R1 9.3% (2025-01) -> gpt-oss-120b 18.5% -> Kimi K2 Thinking 22.3% -> Kimi K2.5 29.4% -> Kimi K2.6 35.9% -> GLM-5.2 40.1% (2026-06). Open lag ~5-7 months and closing. Not saturated but the second derivative is now visible; if you extrapolate, HLE is ~12-18 months from being uninformative. CAVEAT: HLE numbers differ a lot by source (AA has Fable 5 at 53.3%; other aggregators quote 64.5% for the same model on text-only subsets or with tools). Always label the evaluator and the config.
- FrontierMath: MESSY — use with care. Epoch's public data (epoch.ai/data/benchmarks.csv) now has TWO incompatible Tier-4 sets. On the OLD Tier-4 (2025-07-01) the record is 47.9% (DeepMind AI Co-Mathematician, manual run) and GPT-5.5 Pro 39.6%. On the NEW Tier-4 v2 (released 2026-06-12 after "correcting errors in 42% of problems"; 43 problems), the same class of models score 3x higher: Claude Fable 5 87.8%, GPT-5.6 Sol 82.9%, Claude Opus 4.8 56.1% (vs 31.3% on v1). So the flagship "hardest math benchmark" now reads as near-saturated on v2 while Epoch's own blog was still celebrating a 31% record on v1. I am recording both and flagging the inconsistency rather than picking one — do NOT put FrontierMath Tier 4 on a slide without explaining the v1/v2 regrade. Tiers 1-3 v2: GPT-5.6 Sol 89.1%, open-weight GLM-5.2 59.2% — also heading for saturation. Open-weight coverage exists but is sparse (GLM-5.2, Kimi K2.6, Kimi K2.7 Code, DeepSeek-V4-Pro).
- METR 50% time horizon: BEAUTIFUL TREND, WRONG COVERAGE. TH v1.1 yaml: GPT-4 4.0 min (2023-03) -> Claude 3.7 60.4 min -> GPT-5 203 min -> Claude Opus 4.5 293 min -> Claude Opus 4.6 718.8 min (2026-02) -> Claude Mythos Preview (early) 1044.8 min (2026-04, ~17.4 h). Stated doubling time from 2023 on: 128.744 days (CI 104-158), i.e. ~4.3 months, ~50% faster than the original 7-month claim. BUT: (a) only 26 models, essentially zero open-weight models in the v1.1 results file (gpt-oss-120b is discussed in their notes but is not in the results yaml), (b) METR itself warns "Measurements above 16 hrs are unreliable with our current task suite" and the current SOTA point (17.4 h) is already past that line, with a CI of 8.5-55 h. So it cannot be your open-vs-closed benchmark and its top point is now at the measurement ceiling.
- SWE-bench Verified: SATURATING (Epoch: Claude Opus 4.7 83.5%, open-weight GLM-5.2 78.7%, DeepSeek-V4-Pro 77.6% — open is within 5 points of closed). Fine for the "open weights caught up" slide, useless for headroom. Epoch's headline finding is "no signs of improvement" across playthroughs, i.e. it is designed to show a capability that is NOT rising — the wrong story for your talk, but a great counterpoint slide. (v) Epoch/METR "MirrorCode" is referenced by Epoch as a new frontier-coding benchmark but I could not retrieve results for it.

- Every number above was pulled from a machine-readable file I actually fetched, not from rendered HTML: https://epoch.ai/data/benchmarks.csv (993 runs), https://epoch.ai/data/eci_scores.csv (211 models), https://arcprize.org/media/data/leaderboard/v2.json + v3.json (generatedAt 2026-07-09T19:48:54Z), https://metr.org/assets/benchmark_results_1_1.yaml, and the embedded JSON payload of https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/humanitys-last-exam (533 model records with is_open_weights + release_date). All of these are downloadable — you can regenerate the plots yourself and cite the URL.
- CROSS-SOURCE DISCREPANCIES (record them, don't hide them): GLM-5.2 GPQA is 91.9% per Epoch but 89.5% per Artificial Analysis (different harness/prompting). HLE for Claude Fable 5 is 53.3% per AA but third-party aggregators report 64.5% (text-only subset and/or tool use). Terminal-Bench 2.0 top is 84.7% (unverified community agent) vs 82.3% (verified). FrontierMath Tier 4 v1 vs v2 differ by a factor ~2-3 for the same models. Vendor self-reported numbers were deliberately excluded from these records: every record here is from an independent evaluator (Epoch AI, Artificial Analysis, METR, ARC Prize, Scale SEAL, tbench.ai) — except the Terminal-Bench 2.0 community rows, which I have labelled unverified.

- I found no evidence of any benchmark other than ECI that satisfies all three of (unsaturated) + (series back to 2023) + (systematic open-weight coverage). HLE is the closest single benchmark; CritPt is the best physics-flavoured one; METR is the best "agentic capability doubles every ~4.3 months" number but has no open-weight coverage.

verifications.summary:
VERDICT: All 97 records verified. No fabrications found.

METHOD: I did not trust the harvester's quotes or my own (stale) memory. I re-downloaded both source files fresh with curl — https://metr.org/assets/benchmark_results_1_1.yaml (HTTP 200, 16,255 bytes) and https://metr.org/assets/benchmark_results_1_0.yaml (HTTP 200, 14,328 bytes) — parsed them with PyYAML, and mechanically diffed every record against the file: model key existence, p50/p80 estimate, release_date, and (where the quote included them) both CI bounds. I also cross-checked the `scaffolds` field for every record that makes a scaffold-specific claim.

RESULTS: 26 model entries in TH1.1, 33 in TH1.0. Every claimed model key exists. Every score matches to the last decimal. Every release_date matches. Every ci_high/ci_low reproduced in a quote matches the file exactly — a strong anti-fabrication signal, since invented CIs are hard to make self-consistent.

Three records tripped my automated tolerance check; all three are benign, and I verified each by hand against the raw file:
1. davinci-002 p80: claimed 0.06, file says 0.056238. Correct 2-dp rounding, and the quote carries the exact value.
2. GPT-2 p50: claimed 0.05, file says 0.053778. Same — correct 2-dp rounding.
   (For these two, 2-dp rounding is lossy at that magnitude — ~7% high. Use the full-precision values if the numbers feed a fitted curve rather than a slide.)
3. Qwen2-72B p80: claimed 0.6, file says 0.595157. The score is the correct rounding, but the QUOTE misrenders the file as "estimate: 0.595". This is the only record whose quoted text does not appear literally on the page — a truncation, not a wrong number. The harvester had already self-flagged this one as confidence "medium".

NOTES WORTH THE PARENT AGENT'S ATTENTION:
- The four post-cutoff models I was most suspicious of — Claude Mythos Preview (early) at 1044.78 min, Claude Opus 4.6 at 718.81, Gemini 3.1 Pro at 384.15, GPT-5.4 at 341.74 — are all genuinely present in the live TH1.1 YAML with matching dates, estimates, and CIs. My training data has no knowledge of them; the file does. Not fabrications.
- Watch the Mythos and Opus 4.6 confidence intervals before putting them on a slide: Mythos p50 CI is [508.9, 3304.3] and Opus 4.6 p50 CI is [316.7, 3633.8]. Both are enormously wide (Opus 4.6's upper bound is 5x its point estimate). The point estimates are real but very weakly constrained.
- The harvester correctly did NOT conflate the same-named entries that appear in both files with different values: gpt_4 (3.99 in TH1.1 vs 6.02 in TH1.0), o3 (119.73 vs 91.44), o1_preview (20.33 vs 23.25), claude_opus_4_5 (292.99 inspect vs 246.78). These are the exact traps a sloppy or fabricating harvester would fall into, and it didn't.
- The three legacy models (gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct, davinci-002, GPT-2) carry benchmark_name "METR-Horizon-v1.0" even inside the 1_1 file — the harvester's "TH1.0, carried into TH1.1 chart" caveat is accurate, not hand-waving.
